1114.title: Feelings (CCC 1762–1770)
1114.hook: feelings are neither good nor bad in themselves
1114.howItsDone: Catholic teaching treats emotions as a natural part of human life, morally good or bad by how they are chosen and acted on; what is confessed in the sacrament of penance is what a person chose, not what they simply felt.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what makes an act good: the act itself, the intention and the circumstances. Your line was what, why, when.

"And Jesus wept." In the Douay-Rheims that's the whole verse. He's on his way to the tomb of his friend Lazarus, with Lazarus's sister Mary and the mourners, and he cries. The Gospels show him feeling a great deal: moved with pity at a crowd, looking round with anger in a synagogue, grieved at the blindness of hearts. In the garden the night before he dies: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death." Some people grow up thinking a truly good person wouldn't feel anger, or fear, or grief that knocks them flat.
screen: `AND JESUS WEPT.` → `PITY, ANGER, SORROW.` → `IS A STRONG FEELING A FAILURE?`

segments.voice: The Catechism's old word for this is passions. Not a hobby: feelings, emotions, movements inside a person toward something sensed as good, or away from something sensed as bad. Delight, desire, fear, anger, sadness, hope. They're a natural part of being human, it says, a bridge between the body's senses and the mind. Then the sentence today hangs on: in themselves, the passions are neither good nor evil. A feeling isn't a choice yet. Anger rising when someone is mocked is not a sin. Fear before surgery is not a sin. What makes a feeling morally good or bad is what reason and will do with it. Anger can become a hard word or a slammed door. It can also become the courage to speak up. Same feeling, two roads. The most basic passion, the Catechism says, is love, the pull toward what's good, and the others grow from it: desire for a good that's absent, joy in one that's present, fear and sadness at what threatens it. And strong feelings don't decide how holy someone is. Some readers take comfort there: a person can pray with no feeling at all and still be praying. It doesn't ask anyone to stop feeling, either. It quotes a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God." The goal is to be moved toward the good not by the will alone, but by the heart too.

segments.voice: Notice what's moving in you right now, not what you think you should feel: irritation, worry, boredom, tenderness, something without a name. Give it one plain word, silently, and let it be there the way weather is weather, without arguing or scolding; if you pray, hold it out to God as it is. If what's there is a darkness that won't lift, or you don't want to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

1115.title: Forming conscience (CCC 1783–1794)
1115.hook: conscience must be educated and can err
1115.howItsDone: Catholics form their conscience through scripture, prayer, the examination of conscience, advice from others and the Church's moral teaching, and the Church teaches that a certain conscience must always be obeyed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the passions: feelings, neither good nor evil in themselves. Your line was feelings are not sins.

A car on a country road at night. The map on the phone hasn't been updated in a long time, and it speaks in the same calm, certain voice it always uses: in a quarter mile, turn left. The driver turns left. The road is gone: a gate, a field, a sign that says closed. The voice wasn't lying. It was sure. It was also wrong, because nobody had taught it what changed. The Catechism says an inner voice must be followed, and in the same breath, that it can be wrong.
screen: `A CALM, CERTAIN VOICE.` → `THE ROAD IS GONE.` → `SURE, AND WRONG.`

segments.voice: Back on day three hundred ten, you met conscience as the inner sanctuary. Today, how it learns. The Catechism holds two things together. First: a person must always obey the certain judgment of their own conscience; acting deliberately against it is wrong. Second: conscience can make mistakes, so it has to be formed, educated, the way a mind is. It calls this a lifelong task, beginning in childhood. Why? Because people are pulled by bad influences, and tempted to prefer their own judgment and turn from what they're taught. A well-formed conscience is upright and truthful. Then it names the teachers. First, the word of God, taken in through faith and prayer and put into practice: a light for the path, echoing a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths." Alongside it, the gifts of the Spirit, the witness and advice of others, and the Church's authoritative teaching. Then it's honest about error. Sometimes a person really doesn't know better, through no fault of their own; then the wrong isn't held against them, though it's still a wrong. But sometimes ignorance is chosen: a person takes little trouble to find out what's true and good, or habit slowly dulls the conscience. Then the person shares the blame. So conscience is a voice to obey, and a voice to teach. Both at once.

Your line: an educated conscience. Being sure isn't always the same as being right. Until tomorrow.

1116.title: Virtues grow (CCC 1804)
1116.hook: virtues are habits built by repeated good acts
1116.howItsDone: Catholic teaching describes the human virtues as habits acquired by education, deliberate good acts and perseverance, and Catholics work on them through daily practice, the examination of conscience and the sacraments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forming conscience: a voice to obey, and a voice to teach. Your line was an educated conscience.

How does someone become honest? Not by one brave decision on a Monday morning. Watch a baker's apprentice in her first week. The dough sticks to the counter, to her fingers, to her sleeves. The loaves come out flat. Every fold takes thought, and most go wrong. Then another morning, and another, and without anyone marking the moment, something changes. A year on, the same hands fold the dough while she talks about the weather. Nobody gave her that skill in one go. She built it, one sticky morning at a time, until her hands knew before her head did.
screen: `HOW DOES SOMEONE BECOME HONEST?` → `ONE STICKY MORNING AT A TIME.` → `HER HANDS JUST KNOW.`

segments.voice: Back on day three hundred fourteen, you met the four hinges, the cardinal virtues. Today, how virtue grows. The Catechism defines virtue simply: a habitual and firm disposition to do the good. Not one good deed, but a settled way of being, so good acts come more readily. It describes the human virtues as firm attitudes, stable dispositions, habitual perfections of intellect and will. They govern our actions, order our passions, and guide our conduct by reason and faith. Notice the middle one: they order the passions. That picks up two days ago: feelings aren't sins, but they need a shape, and virtue gives them one. And virtue makes possible ease, self-mastery and joy in living a good life. Ease, like the baker who no longer thinks about her hands. The honest person stops arguing with themselves every time a lie would be easier. The virtuous person, the Catechism says, freely practices the good. Then the line behind today's title: these virtues are acquired by human effort. They are the fruit and the seed of morally good acts. Fruit, because good acts repeated build the habit. Seed, because the habit makes the next good act more likely. A circle that turns toward the good. Saint Paul, quoted by the Catechism just before, tells the Philippians to think on whatever is true, just, holy and lovely, if there be any virtue. Think on these things, he says. Then, do them.
screen: `A FIRM HABIT OF DOING GOOD.` · `IT GIVES THE PASSIONS A SHAPE.` · `EASE, SELF-MASTERY AND JOY.` · `THE FRUIT AND THE SEED OF GOOD ACTS.`

Virtue. A firm habit of doing good, built by repeated good acts: the fruit of those acts, and the seed of the next ones. Today's word.
Your line: habits of good. Each good act makes the next one a little easier. See you tomorrow.

1117.title: Gifts and fruits (CCC 1830–1832)
1117.hook: seven gifts of the Spirit, twelve fruits
1117.howItsDone: Catholics associate the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit with baptism and confirmation, where the bishop prays for them, and some learn the gifts and the twelve fruits by heart before confirmation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, virtue: a firm habit of doing good, built one act at a time. Your line was habits of good.

"There shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up out of his root." That's Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims. An old root in the ground, and out of it, something green and new. On that shoot, Isaiah says, the spirit of the Lord will rest, and he names what that spirit brings. Christians have read the passage as being about Jesus, the son of David, born of Jesse's line. The Catechism takes Isaiah's list and says it doesn't stop with him.
screen: `AN OLD ROOT.` → `A SHOOT FROM THE ROOT OF JESSE.` → `THE SPIRIT RESTS ON HIM.`

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred twenty-seven, at confirmation, you met the seven gifts, and on day five hundred eighty-one, the fruits. Today, how they fit. Virtues built by effort, the Catechism says, aren't the whole picture. The moral life is also held up by the gifts of the Holy Spirit: lasting dispositions that make a person docile, ready to follow the Spirit's promptings. Seven: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord. They belong in their fullness to Christ, son of David, and they finish and perfect the virtues of those who receive them. Fortitude is courage that holds. Counsel is knowing what to do in a tangle. Fear of the Lord, as some teachers explain it, isn't terror but awe, the kind that keeps God God. That's the root. Then the fruit. The fruits of the Spirit, the Catechism says, are perfections the Spirit forms in a person, as the first fruits of eternal glory, and the Church's tradition lists twelve, from Galatians. In the Douay-Rheims: "But the fruit of the Spirit is, charity, joy, peace, patience, benignity, goodness, longanimity, mildness, faith, modesty, continency, chastity." Benignity is kindness. Longanimity is long, patient endurance, a slow fuse. Continency is self-control. A gift is received and hidden, like a root. A fruit shows on the branch, where others can see it and be fed. Nobody tastes your fortitude. They taste your patience on a hard afternoon. The gifts are given; the fruits are how anyone can tell.
screen: `THE GIFTS: READY FOR THE SPIRIT.` · `SEVEN GIFTS, FULL IN CHRIST.` · `TWELVE FRUITS, FROM GALATIANS.` · `THE ROOT IS HIDDEN, THE FRUIT FEEDS.`

segments.voice: Go back over the last day or two, slowly, and look for one moment, in you or in someone near you, where one of those fruits showed up: patience in a checkout line, gentleness with a tired child, joy from nowhere, peace in a tense meeting. Gifts and fruits. The gifts of the Spirit, wisdom through fear of the Lord, make a person ready to follow God; the fruits, charity through chastity, are what grows and shows. Today's word.
Your line: gifts become fruit. The root hides; the fruit feeds. Until tomorrow.

1118.title: Mercy and sin (CCC 1846–1848)
1118.hook: the gospel reveals mercy toward sinners
1118.howItsDone: Catholics confess sins to God and, in the sacrament of penance, to a priest, who speaks words of absolution; the Church teaches that God's mercy is offered to every sinner who turns back.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gifts and fruits: the hidden root, and the fruit others can taste. Your line was gifts become fruit.

Joseph is asleep, and troubled. The woman he's engaged to is pregnant, and the child isn't his. He's already decided to send her away quietly. Then, Matthew says, an angel comes to him in a dream, tells him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife, and gives him the child's name before he's born. In the Douay-Rheims: "thou shalt call his name JESUS. For he shall save his people from their sins." Before a single miracle or sermon, the name is about sin, and about rescue from it.
screen: `JOSEPH, TROUBLED, ASLEEP.` → `A NAME BEFORE THE BIRTH.` → `HE SHALL SAVE HIS PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The Catechism starts its teaching on sin with that name, and with a sentence easy to miss: the Gospel is the revelation, in Jesus Christ, of God's mercy to sinners. Notice the order. It doesn't begin with a catalog of wrongs and offer a way out at the end. It begins with mercy, and sin comes into view inside it. The angel's words are its first witness; the second is the Last Supper, where Jesus calls the cup his blood, shed for the forgiveness of sins. Still, mercy isn't cheap. It quotes Saint Augustine: God created us without us, but he did not will to save us without us. Mercy is offered, but it has to be received, and receiving it starts with honesty. The first letter of John, in the Douay-Rheims: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins." So, in this teaching, the admission isn't the price of mercy. It's the open hand that takes it. Last, Paul: "where sin abounded, grace did more abound." But grace, the Catechism says, has to uncover sin in order to heal it, and it borrows an image from Pope John Paul the Second: a physician who probes the wound before treating it. The probing hurts. It's also how a wound gets clean. In this teaching, nobody is asked to earn their way back before they're loved. Mercy is there first.

1119.title: The common good (CCC 1905–1912)
1119.howItsDone: The common good is a central idea of Catholic social teaching, and the Church's documents invoke it when they speak about work, charity, civic life and politics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mercy and sin: the Gospel reveals mercy first, and sin comes into view inside it. Your line was mercy first.

A streetlight at the corner. Nobody owns it. Nobody thanks it. But a nurse walking home from a late shift can see the curb, a kid finds the way back from a friend's house, and an old man takes his dog out without tripping. Next to it: a crosswalk, a park fountain, a library with its doors open, a bus that runs on time. None of these makes anyone happy, exactly. They make it possible for many different people to get on with their lives. When one goes dark, everyone feels it.
screen: `A STREETLIGHT NOBODY OWNS.` → `A CROSSWALK, A LIBRARY, A BUS.` → `WHEN ONE GOES DARK.`

segments.voice: The Catechism calls that whole web the common good. Because people are social by nature, it says, the good of each person is bound up with the good of all. Its definition, borrowed from the Second Vatican Council: the sum of the social conditions that allow people, as groups and as individuals, to reach their fulfillment more fully and more easily. Notice the word conditions. The common good isn't a society deciding what will make each person happy. It's the streetlight, not the walk home: it makes flourishing possible, and leaves the living to the people. The Catechism names three essential parts. First, respect for the person: public authorities must respect basic human rights, including the freedom to act by a sound conscience, the protection of privacy, and rightful freedom in matters of religion. Second, social well-being and development: what a truly human life needs should be within reach, food, clothing, health, work, education and culture, suitable information, the right to start a family. Third, peace: the stability and security of a just order. Then it widens the circle. The human family is one, so there's also a universal common good, reaching across borders; it names refugees and migrants, and migrants' families. And it ends with a reminder that keeps the idea honest: the order of society must serve the good of persons, not the other way around. It quotes Jesus in Mark: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Systems exist for people.
screen: `THE GOOD OF EACH, BOUND TO ALL.` · `CONDITIONS, NOT A SCRIPT FOR HAPPINESS.` · `RESPECT, WELL-BEING, PEACE.` · `A UNIVERSAL COMMON GOOD.`

segments.voice: Walk in your mind through the places you'll pass today, a sidewalk, an office kitchen, a group chat, and look for one thing that belongs to nobody, serves everybody, and could use a hand: litter by a bench, a broken light to report, a sink of shared mugs, a newcomer nobody has greeted. Picture yourself doing it, without anyone noticing. If you pray, offer it for the people who'll never know.
Common good. The social conditions that let people, together and one by one, reach their fulfillment more fully and more easily: respect for the person, well-being, and peace. Today's word.
Your line: everyone flourishing. It starts with things nobody owns. Same time tomorrow.

1120.title: Subsidiarity (CCC 1883–1885)
1120.hook: decisions should be made at the lowest level that can handle them
1120.howItsDone: Subsidiarity is a principle of Catholic social teaching; Catholics invoke it in debates about the roles of families, local communities, charities and governments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the common good: the conditions that let everyone flourish. Your line was everyone flourishing.

Moses sits from morning until evening, and the line of people waiting for him never ends. Every dispute comes to him. His father-in-law, Jethro, watches for a day and says, more or less: this isn't good. You'll wear yourself out, and these people with you. So Jethro gives him a plan, in Exodus. Choose able, honest people, set them over groups large and small, and let them settle the ordinary matters. Only the hard cases come up to you. Moses listens, and does it. The Catechism doesn't tell this story, but it names a principle that sits beside it.
screen: `MORNING UNTIL EVENING.` → `THIS ISN'T GOOD.` → `THE HARD CASES COME UP.`

segments.voice: The word is subsidiarity. The Catechism sets it inside a worry: societies need to work together, but too much intervention by the state can threaten personal freedom and initiative. So the Church's teaching has worked out a principle. A community of a higher order shouldn't interfere in the internal life of a community of a lower order, taking over its functions. It should support it when it needs help, and help coordinate its work with the rest of society, always toward the common good. The family does what a family can do. The neighborhood, the parish, the town, what they can do. The larger body steps in to help, not to swallow. Then the Catechism holds up a model, and it isn't a theory of economics. It's how God governs. God, it says, has not willed to reserve to himself all exercise of power. He entrusts to every creature the functions it is capable of performing, according to its own nature. That way of governing shows great regard for human freedom, and should inspire the wisdom of those who govern communities. Last, the edges. Subsidiarity is opposed to all forms of collectivism, and it sets limits on the state's intervention. Nor is it an excuse for the bigger body to walk away: support in time of need is part of the definition. Yesterday's common good says what society is for. Subsidiarity says who should do it first: the closest hands that can.
screen: `TOO MUCH CONTROL THREATENS FREEDOM.` · `THE LARGER HELPS, IT DOESN'T SWALLOW.` · `GOD SHARES HIS POWER.` · `LIMITS ON THE STATE.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where you tend to take over, a child's homework, a coworker's slides, a partner's way of loading the dishwasher, and ask: can they handle this? If the answer is yes, picture yourself stepping back, hands off, available if they ask, and notice how that feels, maybe relief, maybe itchy fingers. If you pray, ask for the patience to let others do what they can.
Subsidiarity. A higher community shouldn't take over what a smaller one can do, but should help it when it needs help. The Catechism roots it in the way God shares his power. Today's word.
Your line: closest hands first. The week ran from feelings and conscience, through virtue and mercy, to the common good and subsidiarity. And that's seven days.
